subtopics.title: Dispute background and positions
subtopics.summary: The Mahanadi dispute concerns how the river's waters are shared between upstream Chhattisgarh and downstream Odisha. Odisha says upstream construction has reduced its downstream flow, while Chhattisgarh cites its larger catchment share and development needs. The conflict is sharpest in the non-monsoon season and is intensified by the absence of a formal sharing agreement.

subtopics.title: Tribunal status and deadlock
subtopics.summary: The Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal has given both states a final opportunity to agree a water-sharing formula and has issued an ultimatum for a settlement by May 2. If no settlement is reached, the Tribunal will decide on available evidence and legal principles. The Tribunal has voiced dissatisfaction with repeated adjournments, and the deadlock is linked to unreliable data and a trust deficit.

subtopics.title: Legal framework for inter-state waters
subtopics.summary: Article 262 empowers Parliament to adjudicate inter-state river disputes and allows it to exclude courts' jurisdiction in such matters. The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 was used for the Mahanadi tribunal, and the River Boards Act, 1956 provides for river boards. Entries 17 and 56 divide powers between the States and the Union, and the Supreme Court cannot question a tribunal's award but can question its working.

subtopics.title: River course and Hirakud Dam
subtopics.summary: The Mahanadi originates at Sihawa Hill in Raipur, Chhattisgarh, and flows through Odisha before emptying into the Bay of Bengal. It receives left-bank and right-bank tributaries. Hirakud Dam on the river is described in the booklet as the longest earthen dam in the world.

Mahanadi flows through Odisha before emptying into the Bay of Bengal
Left bank tributaries: Shivnath, Hasdeo, Mand and Ib
Right bank tributaries: Jonk, Ong and Tel
Hirakud Dam is the longest earthen dam in the world

subtopics.title: Other inter-state water tribunals
subtopics.summary: India has several inter-state water tribunals, each set up for a particular river dispute. The booklet lists tribunals formed between 1986 and 2018, covering states such as Punjab, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. The Mahanadi tribunal is one of these five.

quizzes.title: Dispute Background Check
quizzes.passage: The Mahanadi water dispute is a conflict between Odisha and Chhattisgarh over how the river's waters should be shared. Odisha, the downstream state, says that extensive upstream constructions in Chhattisgarh have reduced the water flowing into its territory. In Odisha's view, this decline threatens irrigation, drinking water supply, fisheries and the ecological sustainability of the state. Chhattisgarh, the upstream state, argues that it has a legitimate right to utilise river waters. It points out that it accounts for a larger share of the basin's catchment area. It also says its projects are necessary for regional development and water security. The conflict is most sharp during the non-monsoon season, when water availability downstream becomes critically important. A central obstacle is that the two states have no formal water-sharing agreement between them. The dispute grew more serious after upstream infrastructure work expanded, and Odisha took the matter forward by approaching the highest court of the country. Efforts at negotiation have so far not produced a shared formula. Because no agreed rules exist, each state relies on its own reading of how the river's flow should be shared. Both states continue to hold firmly to their positions, and the question of how the water should be divided remains open.

Reason (R): The Supreme Court cannot question the award or formula given by a Water Disputes Tribunal.

questions.explanation: Article 262 gives the power to exclude courts, while the bar on questioning awards is a separate rule, so R does not explain A.

quizzes.title: Tribunal Status Check
quizzes.passage: The Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal has now reached a stage where the two states must act or face a judgment. The Tribunal has granted both Odisha and Chhattisgarh a final opportunity to arrive at a mutually agreed water-sharing formula within a deadline set for this year. If the states fail, the Tribunal has made clear that it will proceed to adjudicate the dispute on the basis of available evidence and legal principles. The Tribunal has also expressed serious dissatisfaction with repeated adjournments and a lack of substantive progress. It observed that no concrete proposals or narrowing of contentious issues have been placed on record, despite assurances of settlement efforts. The deadlock is attributed mainly to two causes: the absence of information that both sides accept as reliable, and a persistent trust deficit between the two states. These problems have made meaningful negotiation and consensus building difficult. Disputes of this kind are handled by tribunals set up for particular rivers and particular groups of states. The Odisha and Chhattisgarh dispute is one such case, and India has several other tribunals that deal with water sharing between neighbouring states. Each tribunal works within its own dispute and its own set of states.
